claims.claim: LLM poetry has a choppy cadence built from constant objective correlatives and persistent enjambment, which makes it recognizable.
claims.quote: Constant objective correlatives and choppy cadence

claims.claim: AI resolves every scene and ties every thread, whereas real novels leave things unresolved.
claims.quote: Every scene ends properly. Everything tied up nice and tidy
claims.page: The Real Reason Not to Use AI to Write Your Novel

claims.claim: AI stories favor single-track plots with protagonist-driven resolution (69% vs 46% human) and no subplots (79% vs 57%), while human protagonists' choices are framed as more morally ambiguous and human stories show more temporal complexity.
claims.quote: AI stories over-explain themes and favor tidy, single-track plots
claims.page: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction

claims.claim: The model resolves tension because it cannot tell which tension a story needs to keep active; it wants the answer legible where the story needs pressure left unresolved (commentary on StoryScope, not independent of it).
claims.quote: The machine wants to make the answer legible
claims.page: The AI Tells Are in the Story

claims.claim: AI endings resolve ambiguity rather than trusting the reader to hold it.
claims.page: I Asked the Machine to Tell on Itself: A Field Guide to AI Tells

claims.claim: Fiction needs events that surprise then feel inevitable, and earlier details that get re-valued by later ones; autoregressive generation coordinates neither well over length.
claims.source: Katherine Elkins, The AI Fiction Paradox, arXiv 2603.13545 (2026-03-13)
claims.quote: fiction repeatedly requires the significance of earlier details to be reinterpreted

claims.claim: LLM poems force closure with contrived mic-drop final lines.
claims.quote: contrived mic-drops like the last sentence

claims.claim: Negative parallelism in two shapes, 'not just X but Y' and 'not X but Y', is a catalogued sign of AI writing.
claims.source: Wikipedia editors, Signs of AI writing
claims.quote: not a mirror but a portal: not representation, but mechanism

claims.claim: The construction fails cognitively: readers process the negated concept first and retain it, so the reframe lands weaker than the writer intends and compounds with repetition.
claims.quote: Your brain doesn't skip to the alternative.
claims.page: Slanguage: Why AI's stylistic negation is both annoying and doesn't work

claims.claim: In AI fiction the 'not X; Y' construction feels obligatory rather than natural, often alongside stacked triplets of descriptors.
claims.page: How to Identify AI-Written Web Fiction

claims.claim: The negation reframe borrows the sound of insight without delivering it.
claims.quote: It tries to sound sophisticated without being sophisticated.
claims.page: Don't Write Like AI (1 of 101): Negation

claims.claim: The 'isn't just X; it's Y' frame combined with a metaphor and a tricolon is a signature machine sentence that carries no content.
claims.quote: It says absolutely nothing at all.

claims.claim: AI narrators explicitly comment on the story's theme 77% of the time versus 52% for humans, with tighter thematic unity and more central moral questions.
claims.page: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction

claims.claim: AI spells out meaning that human fiction leaves implied; the tell lives in the story's structure, not its word choice.
claims.page: The AI Tells Are in the Story

claims.claim: LLM verse refuses to state itself plainly yet re-restates its load-bearing moments, over-explaining what it has already shown.
claims.quote: Refusal to state itself too plainly, but tendency to re-restate

verdicts.trueWording: The constant objective correlatives and choppy cadence
verdicts.note: Quote is word-for-word (page drops leading 'The'). Enjambment is separately supported on the page: 'The terse, constantly enjambed lines lacked adjectives.' The claim's causal framing (cadence 'built from' correlatives and enjambment) is the summarizer's synthesis; the page lists them as co-occurring tells.

verdicts.trueWording: Every scene ends properly. Every arc gets closed. Everything tied up
verdicts.note: Not verbatim: the quote splices two non-adjacent sentences and drops 'Every arc gets closed.' and 'with a big bow.' Substance fully supported: 'Real novels leave things hanging, unresolved, messier than when they started.'

verdicts.trueWording: AI stories over-explain themes and favor tidy, single-track plots
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the abs-page abstract. All four statistics confirmed in the full text (arxiv.org/html/2604.03136v6, sec 4.1): 'more protagonist-driven resolutions (69% vs. 46%), and far fewer subplots (79% "no subplots" vs. 57%)'; moral ambivalence 59% vs 38%; abstract confirms human 'increased temporal complexity'.

verdicts.trueWording: The machine wants to make the answer legible
verdicts.note: Verbatim. The mechanism half of the claim is also verbatim on the page: 'It resolves because it does not know which tension should remain active.' The parenthetical is correct - the post is explicitly commentary on the StoryScope paper plus an Ethan Mollick X thread, not independent research.

verdicts.trueWording: The model does not trust the reader with ambiguity
verdicts.note: No quote was supplied in the claim record, so verbatim is not in play. Page supports it almost exactly, under the tell 'Resolution bias: endings tie up. The model does not trust the reader with ambiguity unless explicitly told to.'

verdicts.trueWording: fiction repeatedly requires the significance of earlier details to be reinterpreted
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the abstract. Surprise-then-inevitable is also supported: 'events must feel both surprising in the moment and retrospectively inevitable', with 'Standard autoregressive generation... creating a practical obstacle to coordinating' them. Minor overreach: the abstract pins autoregression to challenge one only; the revaluation failure is described as unreliable long-range reasoning, so 'coordinates neither' slightly overstates.

verdicts.trueWording: it loves contrived mic-drops like the last sentence
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim within that sentence. 'Force closure' and 'final lines' are the summarizer's gloss - the source is a parenthetical self-referential joke about its own last sentence, listed among LLM-poetry tells.

verdicts.trueWording: not a mirror but a portal: not a representation of self
verdicts.note: Quote is compressed, not verbatim: the page reads 'Kusama's self-portrait is not a mirror but a portal: not a representation of self, but a mechanism for its constant reinvention.' Claim substance is exact - the page carries a 'Negative parallelisms' section (WP:AIPARALLEL) with subsections 'Not just X, but also Y' and 'Not X, but Y'.

verdicts.trueWording: your brain doesn't skip to the alternative
verdicts.note: Verbatim (mid-sentence in the source, so lowercase 'your'; it also appears as a photo caption). Every element of the claim is on the page: 'It processes the negated concept first', a cited 2003 study where 'readers' mental models still retained the negated concept', 'negation doesn't work the way speakers intend it to', and 'that cognitive load compounds with repetition'.

verdicts.trueWording: The aforementioned "not X; Y" is still universal
verdicts.note: No quote supplied. The page catalogues the construction and puts 'Lists of three' as the very next item in the same tell list, so the triplet adjacency holds. But the page says the construction is 'universal', never that it 'feels obligatory rather than natural' - that characterization is the summarizer's, and the nearest support is the essay calling such passages 'tryhard'.

verdicts.trueWording: It tries to sound sophisticated without being sophisticated
verdicts.note: Verbatim. Context supports the claim: the author reports Claude's own explanation that 'Negation adds depth to statements, making content sound more sophisticated', then delivers the quoted line as the rebuttal.

verdicts.trueWording: it says absolutely nothing at all
verdicts.note: Words appear verbatim but as a clause, not a sentence: 'The kind you skim past, then return only to discover it says absolutely nothing at all.' Referent nuance - that line is the article's opener about nondescript machine prose generally; the 'isn't just X; it's Y' + metaphor + tricolon template is introduced separately, credited to Elizabeth Goodspeed as 'a particularly grating pattern' with the template spelled out verbatim.

Verbatim, but in the paper's full text (sec 4.1 heading, arxiv.org/html/2604.03136v6), not on the cited /abs/ landing page, whose abstract instead reads 'AI stories over-explain themes'. All statistics confirmed: 'Narrators explicitly explain the story's theme 77% of the time, versus 52% for humans', 'with tighter thematic unity and more central moral questions'; Table 16 gives Narratorial Thematic Commentary 52% human / 77% AI.

Verbatim on the page, but second-hand: the Dramatica post quotes it from a reply by Mohammad Siam, X, May 27, 2026, not as its own formulation. The rest of the claim is the post's own thesis - it moves the conversation 'from punctuation to narrative construction' and quotes StoryScope's 'AI spells out meaning'.

verdicts.trueWording: a refusal to state itself too plainly, but a tendency
verdicts.note: Not verbatim: the quote drops both articles. Page reads 'A refusal to state itself too plainly, but a tendency to re-restate its load-bearing moments.' Substance fully supported, including 'over-explaining what it has already shown' via 're-restate its load-bearing moments'.
